Brewer's sparrow (Spizella breweri) commences its life cycle when the female deposits a clutch averaging 3.8 eggs per nesting attempt [N_R_i = 3.8 eggs per nesting attempt]. Field studies conducted across the sagebrush ecosystems of the Great Basin indicate that females typically complete two broods per breeding season [F_R_i = two broods per breeding season], a reproductive strategy that appears linked to the ephemeral abundance of arthropod prey during the late spring months. Eggs are incubated by the female alone over a period of approximately 12 days [ab = approximately 12 days] at a mean nest temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. The hatchling emerges at a wet weight of just 1.45 grams [Wwb = 1.45 grams], a diminutive body mass consistent with the altricial mode of development characteristic of emberizid sparrows. This initial mass is only marginally greater than the weight of the freshly laid egg, which is recorded at 1.38 grams [Ww0 = 1.38 grams]. The progression from a fertilized ovum to a free-living fledgling thus depends critically upon the female's capacity to maintain consistent incubation temperatures throughout the developmental period.

Following hatching, the altricial nestling enters a period of rapid somatic growth fueled by frequent provisioning from both parents. Under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods in this species (41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]), the developing chick achieves the milestone of fledging at 7 days after hatching [tx = 7 days after hatching]. This brief nestling phase, lasting only a single week from the time since birth at fledging (7 days since birth) [tx = 7 days since birth], is among the shortest recorded for a North American sparrow of comparable body size at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. The rapidity of this transition likely reflects strong selective pressure from nest predation, which is substantial in sagebrush habitats. During this period, the chick's mass increases dramatically; the ultimate wet weight of an adult Brewer's sparrow is reported to be 12.5 grams [Wwi = 12.5 grams], placing the species near the lower end of the mass range for the genus Spizella. Some individuals, particularly those in more productive northern portions of the range, may attain a slightly higher mass of up to 14 grams.

Sexual maturation in Brewer's sparrow proceeds relatively quickly compared to many other migratory passerines. Puberty, defined as the onset of functional gonadal activity, is reached at 21 days after hatching [tp = 21 days after hatching] when individuals are maintained at an ambient temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. It is important to note that the time since birth at puberty (21 days since birth) [tp = 21 days since birth] is calculated from the point of hatching, not from egg-laying, reflecting the developmental window during which the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis becomes fully active at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This early onset of reproductive capability is somewhat misleading from an ecological perspective, however, because young birds do not typically engage in breeding activities during their first summer. Instead, individuals delay their first successful reproductive attempt until the following spring, a constraint imposed by the need to acquire a breeding territory and accumulate sufficient body condition for the demands of egg production and incubation.

The first successful breeding event for a Brewer's sparrow typically occurs at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching], a temporal lag that reflects the obligate migratory cycle of the species under thermal conditions of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This means that the time since birth at first brood (365 days since birth) [tR = 365 days since birth] effectively synchronizes with the bird's second calendar year of life at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. After completing a post-fledging molt and a southward migration to wintering grounds in Mexico and the southwestern United States, the immature bird returns to its natal region the following spring. Upon arrival at the breeding grounds, males establish territories through advertisement song, while females assess habitat quality and mate quality before initiating nest construction. The delay between reaching puberty at 21 days and actually producing a first brood at 365 days represents one of the most pronounced gaps between physiological maturity and realized reproduction documented among North American sparrows.

Maximum longevity for Spizella breweri in the wild is estimated at approximately 6.2 years [am = approximately 6.2 years], a value derived from recapture records of banded individuals at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Recapture data from banding studies suggest that maximum lifespan is approximately 2263 days [am = approximately 2263 days] at a body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This relatively short lifespan, typical of a small-bodied passerine with high annual adult mortality, is consistent with the species' rapid life-history strategy: early fledging at 7 days, early puberty at 21 days, and a high annual reproductive investment of two broods per season. The trade-off between current reproduction and survival is evident in the energetic costs of repeated nesting attempts across the breeding season. From a demographic perspective, the combination of a 3.8 egg clutch [N_R_i = 3.8 egg clutch] and two broods annually [F_R_i = two broods annually] yields a substantial annual fecundity that compensates for the elevated mortality rates experienced by both adults and juveniles during migration and winter residency.
